documents.t: Each page here covers one task, in the order you'd hit them: a server has to exist before you can register a publisher, and a table has to exist before anything can transform it. For worked end-to-end projects against real systems, see Advanced Tutorials.

Before you begin Create a Project A collection holds functions and the tables they write. The group it is created in decides which kind of function it can hold, and that is fixed for the collection's life. A source or destination collection also carries exactly one connection, and it is created together with that connection rather than separately. Step 1Create a data product collection, for transformers tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name reporting \ --group default \ --description "Reporting tables" A collection in default, or in any group you created, holds transformers and takes no connection. Passing --conn-file here is an error. Step 2Or create a source collection, with its connection tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml --conn-file is required for sources and destinations. The CLI derives the group from the connection's direction, so --group acts as an assertion: a mismatch is an error rather than a preference. Step 3Confirm it exists tdk collection list --proj finance tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_src tdk collection get prints a data product collection's type as Data Factory, which is the same thing the docs call a data product.

--storage-path is the logical prefix for the collection's artifacts, written as base_path in the API. Unset, it inherits the project's prefix, and the resolved value is readable as effective_base_path. Changing it later is not retroactive: existing data versions keep the path they were written under, and only new artifacts use the new prefix.

Register a function into the collection. A source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. See tdk collection create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection Deleting a collection deletes its functions and tables, and freezes functions elsewhere that read from it. It takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what depends on the collection tdk table list --proj finance --coll sales_src Functions in other collections that read these tables are frozen by the delete, so it is worth knowing which tables those are. Step 2Delete it tdk collection delete \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src --confirm takes the literal string delete.

The delete is a soft delete with a cascade, in this order: The collection row is renamed to deleted_<id>, which frees the original name for immediate reuse. Functions in other collections that depend on its tables are set to Frozen. A frozen function stays registered and stops running until it is re-registered against tables that exist. Its tables, triggers and dependencies are set to Deleted, and its own functions are set to Deleted. Scheduled cron and stage workers are stopped. After the commit, the connection's stored content is deleted on a best-effort basis. Function status is one of Active, Frozen or Deleted, so a frozen function is visible in a listing rather than silently gone. See tdk collection delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection tdk collection update changes a collection's name, its description, its storage path, or the connection it carries. What it cannot change is the collection's type or the group it belongs to: both are fixed at creation. Step 1Rename it, or change its description tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --new-name sales_source \ --description "Postgres sales tables" Renaming a source or destination collection renames its connection too, since the connection is named by the collection. Step 2Or replace the connection tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --conn-file conn-postgres-prod.yaml The connector kind is fixed for the collection's life, so the replacement document has to be the same kind. Pointing a publisher at a different database means a new connection of the same kind, not a different connector. Step 3Check the result tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_source A request that changes nothing is rejected: The collection update request has nothing to update. When a rename and a connection change are passed together, the rename is applied first.

The collection's type, and therefore its group, are immutable. There is no command that moves a collection to another group, and CollectionUpdate carries no field for it. Changing connectors means deleting the collection and creating it again. --storage-path applies to new artifacts only. Existing data versions keep the path stamped at write time. See tdk collection update for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A group sits inside a project and holds collections. Which group a collection is created in fixes what that collection can hold, and that choice is permanent. Three groups exist in every project already: sources for publishers, destinations for subscribers, and default for transformers. A group you create yourself holds transformers too, so the reason to add one is organising a pipeline rather than unlocking anything new. Step 1Create the group tdk group create \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --description "Raw ingested data" --proj names the project the group belongs to, and can be omitted when a project is pinned. Collections created in bronze hold transformers, the same as default. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups are listed alongside it. System groups cannot be renamed or deleted.

Collections in a user-created group hold transformers, which default already does, so grouping is organisational. The medallion layout, bronze then silver then gold, is a common convention for naming the stages of a pipeline; it is a docs convention rather than something Tabsdata enforces.
documents.s: Why add a group at all

documents.t: Create a Collection in the group. See tdk group create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group Deleting a group deletes the collections inside it. Like the other deletes, it takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what the group holds tdk collection list --proj finance --group bronze Every collection listed here goes with the group. Step 2Delete it tdk group delete \ --proj finance \ --name bronze --confirm takes the literal string delete. The three system groups cannot be deleted, so this only ever applies to a group you created.

The group's collections are deleted with it, along with their tables and functions. Functions in other collections that depended on those tables are frozen rather than deleted: they stay registered and stop running until they are re-registered against tables that exist. See tdk group delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group tdk group update changes a group's name or description. The collections inside it are untouched, and so is what those collections are allowed to hold. Step 1Rename the group, or change its description tdk group update \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --new-name raw \ --description "Raw ingested data" --name is the current name and --new-name the replacement. Either --new-name or --description is enough on its own. Step 2Check the result tdk group get --proj finance --name raw The three system groups, default, sources and destinations, cannot be updated at all.

A collection's type follows from the group it was created in, and renaming the group does not revisit that. A collection created in sources still holds publishers after the group is called something else. See tdk group update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: Before you begin Start a Server A project is the outermost resource within Tabsdata server and allows full isolation from workflows and resources in other projects. Step 1Create the project tdk project create \ --name finance \ --description "Subscription billing" --name starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits or underscores, up to 100 characters, and has to be unique on the server. --description is optional and capped at 200 characters. Step 2Confirm it exists and see its groups tdk project list tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups appear straight away. A collection created in sources holds publishers, one in destinations holds subscribers, and one in default or any group you add yourself holds transformers.

Most commands take --proj to say which project they act on. Pinning one makes it the default: tdk project pin --name finance Every later command then acts on finance unless it passes --proj explicitly.
documents.s: Pin it, so later commands need no --proj

documents.t: A project on its own holds nothing. Create a collection in one of its groups: Create a Collection. See tdk project create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project warning Deleting a project deletes all resources nested inside of it, including function code, execution logs, and table data. This action cannot be reversed. Step 1Check what the project holds tdk group list --proj finance tdk collection list --proj finance Step 2Delete it tdk project delete \ --name finance --confirm takes the literal string delete. Anything else, including y or yes, cancels the command and leaves the project standing.

Every group and collection in the project is deleted with it, along with the tables those collections held and the functions registered in them. The project's name is freed and can be reused immediately. See tdk project delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk project update changes a project's name or its description. Both are metadata: renaming a project does not move, rebuild or re-path anything inside it. Step 1Rename the project, or change its description tdk project update \ --name finance \ --new-name billing \ --description "Subscription billing and dunning" --name names the project as it stands now; --new-name is what it becomes. Passing only --description changes the description and leaves the name alone. Step 2Check the result tdk project get --name billing A request that changes nothing is rejected rather than silently accepted, with The project update request has nothing to update.

The project keeps its id, its groups, its collections and their data. Anything referring to the project by id keeps working; anything referring to it by name, a pinned project or a script passing --proj, needs the new name. See tdk project update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project This tutorial shows how to set up an Amazon S3 publisher that reads one or more files out of an S3 bucket and writes them into one or more Tabsdata Tables

A Connection is a resource that stores the configuration and credentials needed to access an external system. Publishers use the credentials stored in a connection to authenticate with AWS. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3.yaml The file lands in your working directory under the file name specified in the cli command. Step 2Fill in the bucket, the region, and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Fill in the bucket name, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, and base path. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

The connection file in the previous step is passed into Tabsdata by binding it to a Collection. The tdk collection create command takes 3 arguments name: unique name for the collection group: group name to store collection in. Publishers can only be stored in the sources group conn-file: path to .yaml connection file created in previous step. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name hr_files --group sources --conn-file conn-s3.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in hr_files from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it. To point the same publisher code at a different bucket, register it into a second source collection whose connection names that bucket. The code stays untouched.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=["departments.csv", "employees.csv"], ), output_tables=["departments", "employees"], ) def read_files( departments: TableFramesSpec, employees: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (departments[0], employees[0]) Each entry in paths fills one function argument with a list of frames (TableFramesSpec), one frame per matched file. An exact key matches one file, so its slot is a single-element list, which is why the example returns departments[0]. The function returns one frame per name in output_tables, in the same order. Paths resolve relative to the connection's base_path, so the publisher names objects and never the bucket. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll hr_files --name read_files Tabsdata imports the matching files on the server and writes one versioned table per path. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll hr_files tdk table data --coll hr_files --name departments

documents.t: function.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=[ "landing/invoices.parquet", ], ), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_invoices(invoices: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is None: return (None,) return (invoices[0],) paths:list[str]required format:SrcFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional initial_last_modified:datetime | Noneoptional file_info:FileInfo | Noneoptional src_cfg:dict[str, Any]optional trigger_by:list[str] | CronTriggeroptional on_tables:list[DataQuality]optional

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the publisher should poll the bucket on a fixed UTC schedule. The cron mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, with optional start and end bounds for a limited run window. This fits when producers drop files into S3 on their own rhythm and Tabsdata should check hourly, nightly, or on another predictable cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=["landing/invoices.parquet"], ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices[0],)

Set initial_last_modified to ingest only new files instead of re-reading everything on every run. The first run imports files modified at or after the timestamp, and the cutoff advances on its own afterwards, so each trigger imports only what arrived since the previous one. A path that matches no new files fills its slot with None rather than an empty list. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=S3Src(paths=["landing/invoices.parquet"]), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_when_available(invoices: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is None: return (None,) return (invoices[0],)

Access denied or authentication errors. Secrets are read out of the connection file when the collection is created, so an edit made after that point has not reached the server. Re-run tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml to check the document, then tdk collection update --conn-file conn-s3.yaml to send the corrected credentials. Check too that the key pair has read access to the bucket and the prefix. No files imported. Paths are relative to the connection's base_path, so check the path against it. With initial_last_modified set, files older than the current cutoff are skipped by design. Wrong columns or parse errors. The format comes from the file extension. Force it with format and tune parsing with format_cfg. A run succeeds but a table has no new version. Its path matched no new files and the function returned None for that slot, which means keep the current version.

Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: Azure Blob publishers can be driven by a schedule or by another Tabsdata table. Pick the mode that matches how files arrive in the container. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the container should be scanned on a fixed cadence for newly uploaded blobs. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.azureblob import AzureBlobSrc @publisher( source=AzureBlobSrc( paths=["landing/invoices_*.parquet"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices[0],)

Use relative blob paths in AzureBlobSrc(paths=[...]). Format selection, wildcard expansion, initial_last_modified, and file_info behave the same way as the S3 file connector. In practice: Use a stable base_path for the collection and keep publisher paths relative under it. Use wildcard patterns when upstream processes upload many partitioned files. Prefer file_info="uri" when the blob path should survive into downstream processing.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Databricks connector lets a publisher read data out of Databricks and land it in Tabsdata as versioned tables. Each entry in queries produces one output table. A query can carry {placeholder} names that initial_values fills in, so one publisher reads the same tables out of a different catalog or schema without the SQL changing.

The connection holds the workspace URL, the token, the staging volume, and the warehouse the read goes through. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type databricks-bulk-in --file conn-databricks.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the workspace URL, token, volume, and warehouse tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.databricks:DatabricksSrcConn spec: host_url: 'secret:https://dbc-00000000.cloud.databricks.com' token: 'secret:dapi0example0token0000' volume: 'main.default.tabsdata_stage' host_url:Secretrequired token:Secretrequired volume:strrequired warehouse:stroptional warehouse_id:stroptional catalog:stroptional schema:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-databricks.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why there is no separate collection step ahead of this one and why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name world --group sources --conn-file conn-databricks.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in world from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_world.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.country", "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.city", ], initial_values={"catalog": "main", "schema": "default"}, ), output_tables=["country", "city"], ) def read_world( country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (country, city) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll world --path read_world.py::read_world Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll world --name read_world Tabsdata runs the queries on the server and writes one versioned table per query. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll world tdk table data --coll world --name city

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project A log file arrives as one text column, which is the wrong shape for anything downstream to query. grok turns that column into typed columns by matching a pattern with named captures against every row, so a publisher reading log files parses them on the way in and lands a table with real columns instead of raw lines. The pattern syntax follows the Elasticsearch implementation. For the pattern reference, see the Elasticsearch Grok documentation and the predefined pattern library.
documents.s: Publish data from log files with Grok

documents.t: Log files sit on disk or in object storage, so the connection is a file connection rather than anything grok-specific. A local directory: Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type local-file-in --file conn-logs.yaml Step 2Point base_path at the log directory conn-logs.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/var/log/acme' Reading logs out of a bucket instead means s3-file-in or az-file-in here. Nothing else on this page changes: the parsing happens in the publisher body, not in the connection.
Step 3Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name log_src --group sources --conn-file conn-logs.yaml

grok takes three things: the column holding the text, a pattern string, and a schema mapping each capture to an output column and type. A capture is written %{NAME:alias}, where NAME is a predefined pattern such as IPV4, WORD or INT, and alias is the capture name the schema keys on. The full form is %{name:alias:extract:definition}, where definition supplies a regular expression when name is not one of the predefined patterns, and extract is reserved and unused. An Apache access line, parsed into five columns: read_access_logs.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc, SrcFileFormat import tabsdatak.tableframe as tdf import tabsdatak as td PATTERN = ( r"%{IPV4:client_ip} " r"%{USER:ident} " r"%{USER:auth} " r"\[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] " r'"%{WORD:method} ' r'%{URIPATHPARAM:request} ' r'HTTP/%{NUMBER:http_version}" ' r"%{INT:response_code} %{INT:bytes}" ) SCHEMA = { "client_ip": tdf.Column("ip_address", td.String), "method": tdf.Column("http_method", td.String), "response_code": tdf.Column("status_code", td.Int32), "bytes": tdf.Column("response_bytes", td.Int64), "timestamp": tdf.Column("request_time", td.String), } @publisher( source=LocalFileSrc( paths=["access.log"], format=SrcFileFormat.CSV, format_cfg={ SrcFileFormat.CSV: {"has_header": False, "separator": "\\x00"}, }, ), output_tables=["access_logs"], ) def read_access_logs(lines: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if lines is None: return (None,) return (lines[0].grok("column_1", PATTERN, SCHEMA),) The reader has to deliver each log line whole, which is why the CSV options turn the header off and set a separator that does not occur in the text. Without that, a comma inside a log line splits it into columns before grok sees it. The schema keys are capture names and the values are output columns, so a capture the schema leaves out is matched and discarded. That is how ident, auth, request and http_version stay out of the resulting table while still being required by the pattern. Step 4Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll log_src --path read_access_logs.py::read_access_logs

documents.t: A long pattern makes it easy to write a schema key that no capture produces. grok_fields returns the capture names a pattern generates, in order, so the schema can be written against the real list rather than a guess: check_pattern.py from tabsdatak.expansions.tableframe.features.grok.engine import grok_fields pattern = r"%{WORD:action}-%{INT:year}-%{WORD:action}-%{INT:year}" captures = grok_fields(pattern) # ['action', 'year', 'action[1]', 'year[1]'] Repeated capture names are disambiguated with a bracketed index, starting at 1 for the second occurrence. Both names have to appear in the schema for both captures to reach the table: repeated_captures.py SCHEMA = { "action": tdf.Column("first_name", td.String), "action[1]": tdf.Column("second_name", td.String), "year": tdf.Column("first_year", td.Int64), "year[1]": tdf.Column("second_year", td.Int64), }
documents.s: Finding out what a pattern captures

documents.t: A row the pattern fails to match is kept, with null in every grok column. Nothing is dropped and the run does not fail, so a table with a block of nulls across the parsed columns means the pattern stopped matching rather than that the source went empty. Counting those nulls after a run is the quickest check that a pattern still fits a log format that changed: tdk table data --coll log_src --name access_logs

Every parsed column is null. The pattern does not match the lines. Read one raw line and walk it against the pattern; a changed log format usually breaks at the first literal separator. A schema key raises an error. The key is not a capture the pattern produces. Run grok_fields on the pattern and use the names it returns, including the bracketed ones. Lines arrive already split into several columns. The file reader parsed them as delimited text. Set has_header off and a separator that does not occur in the log lines.

Access denied / authentication errors: secrets are read out of the connection file when the collection is created, so an edit made after that point has not reached the server. With transactional=True (the default) all queries share one transaction, so a partial set of tables never lands. A run succeeds but a table has no new version: its query matched no rows and the function returned None for that slot, which means keep the current version. See None, and "no new version".

documents.t: function.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf @publisher( source=PostgresSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000", ], ), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_invoices(invoices: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is not None: last_id = invoices.select(tdf.col("id").max()).one()["id"] ctx.set_attr("last_id", last_id) return (invoices,) queries:list[str]required transactional:booloptional schema_overrides:list[dict | None]optional initial_values:dict[str, Any]optional src_cfg:dict[str, Any]optional trigger_by:list[str] | CronTriggeroptional on_tables:list[DataQuality]optional

Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the publisher should poll PostgreSQL on a fixed UTC schedule. Instead of re-reading a whole table every run, a query can page through it: The :last_id bind takes its value from initial_values on the first run, and from ctx on every run after that. After reading a batch, store the highest id seen with ctx.set_attr("last_id", ...). Values set on ctx are persisted and become the same-named bind's value on the next run, so each trigger continues past the last row read. When the query returns no new rows the slot arrives as None. Returning (None,) keeps the table's current version and leaves the watermark untouched. Compare with a strict > against a unique, monotonically increasing column, a serial key or a commit timestamp, and pair it with ORDER BY and LIMIT so each run reads one bounded, ordered page. With >= the last row of one run is re-read by the next. Queries can use any number of named binds. Seed each one in initial_values and advance whichever ones you set on ctx.

A query that matches no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty table. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=PostgresSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM city WHERE 1 = 0"]), output_tables=["city"], ) def read_when_available(city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (city,)

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project A Salesforce publisher runs SOQL queries against a Salesforce org and lands each result as a versioned table. Each entry in queries produces one output table, so the query list and the table list line up position by position. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[salesforce]'
documents.s: Publish data from a Salesforce SOQL query

documents.t: The connection holds the org credentials: a username, a password, and a security token. The username is the Salesforce username rather than the email address on the account, which is the mistake that most often produces an authentication failure on a first attempt. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type salesforce-sosql-in --file conn-salesforce.yaml Step 2Fill in the username, password, and security token conn-salesforce.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceSrcConn spec: credentials: kind: salesforceTokenCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:SalesforceToken spec: username: 'secret:integration@acme.com' password: 'secret:example-password' security_token: 'secret:exampleSecurityToken00' To find the security token, open View Profile in Salesforce, go to Settings, and choose Reset My Security Token. Salesforce mails the new token and invalidates the old one, so reset it only when you are ready to update the connection. instance_url is optional and belongs on the connection when one set of credentials maps to more than one org. Left out, the instance is inferred from the username and password. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-salesforce.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name sf_src --group sources --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_sales.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=[ "SELECT Id, AccountId, FirstName, LastName, Email, SystemModStamp " "FROM Contact WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified", "SELECT Name, Type, SystemModStamp " "FROM Account WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified", ], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts", "accounts"], ) def read_sales( contacts: TableFramesSpec, accounts: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (contacts[0], accounts[0]) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sf_src --path read_sales.py::read_sales Re-register after every code change.
Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll sf_src --name read_sales Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll sf_src tdk table data --coll sf_src --name contacts
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: Every Salesforce object carries a SystemModStamp column, and Tabsdata reads it to publish only the rows that changed since the previous run. Two things have to be true for that to work: SystemModStamp appears in the SELECT list, and the WHERE clause compares it against the $lastModified placeholder. On the first run $lastModified takes the value of initial_last_modified. On every later run it takes the highest SystemModStamp seen so far, so each trigger reads forward from where the last one stopped. Deletions are invisible to that comparison, because a deleted row stops appearing rather than getting a newer timestamp. Set include_deleted to True to read deleted records too, which is what makes an incremental load able to tell that a row went away.

Parameter Required What it does queries yes SOQL queries, one per output table, in order initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run include_deleted no Reads deleted records as well. Defaults to False instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several version no Salesforce API version. Defaults to the latest

A query that returns no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty frame. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one, which is the usual outcome of an incremental run with nothing new to read: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Email, SystemModStamp FROM Contact " "WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts"], ) def read_when_available(contacts: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if contacts is None: return (None,) return (contacts[0],)

Authentication fails. Check that the username is the Salesforce username and not the email address, and that the security token matches the current password. Resetting either one invalidates the token. Every run re-reads everything. The query is missing $lastModified in its WHERE clause, or SystemModStamp is missing from the SELECT list. Both are required for the incremental read. Rows disappear from the source but stay in the table. include_deleted defaults to False, so deletions are not read at all. Wrong org. One set of credentials that maps to several orgs needs instance_url on the connection to pick between them.

documents.s: Trigger it and read the table

documents.t: report takes one report or a list of them, referenced by id or by name. Which of the two is meant is inferred from the value, and find_report_by states it outright when the inference would guess wrong. A report referenced by name uses what Salesforce calls the report unique name, also shown as the developer name, rather than the label displayed in the UI. column_name_strategy decides where the output column names come from. A Salesforce report carries both a columnName and a label for every column: CREATED_ALIAS against alias, for instance. The choice sets the column names in the resulting Tabsdata table, and it also sets the names the filters have to use, so a filter written against labels breaks when the strategy is columnName.
documents.s: Naming a report, and naming its columns

documents.t: Each filter is a tuple of a column, an operator, and a value, in the form Salesforce report queries already use. More than one filter goes in a list. filter_logic states how those filters combine, referring to them by position: the first filter in the list is 1, the second is 2, and so on. "1 or 2" accepts a row matching either, and "1 or (2 and 3)" groups them. Without filter_logic, the filters carry no stated relationship between them.

initial_last_modified sets where the first run starts, as a string in Salesforce datetime format with the timezone included. last_modified_column names the column the comparison runs against, and that column has to be in the report for the read to work. It defaults to None, which reads the whole report on every run.

Parameter Required What it does report yes One report or a list, by id or by name column_name_strategy yes columnName or label, setting output column names find_report_by no id or name, when the reference is ambiguous filter no Tuples of column, operator, value filter_logic no How the filters combine, by position initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run last_modified_column no Report column driving the incremental read instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several

A filter matches nothing. Filters use whichever names column_name_strategy selected, so a filter written against alias fails under columnName and needs CREATED_ALIAS instead. The report is not found by name. Salesforce matches the report unique name, not the label in the UI. Set find_report_by to name and pass the unique name, or reference the report by id. Every run re-reads the whole report. last_modified_column is unset, or the column it names is missing from the report definition.

Combine rows from two or more Tabsdata Tables. A transformer declares one input_tables entry per table and takes a parameter for each.

concat() stacks TableFrames by appending their rows. how decides what happens when the inputs do not line up: verticalvertical_relaxeddiagonaldiagonal_relaxed The default, so it can be left off. Every input must share the same columns and the same types. concat.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @transformer( input_tables=["sales_east", "sales_west"], output_tables=["sales_all"], ) def transform(east: TableFrameSpec, west: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = concat([east, west]) return result sales_east region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 2 rows sales_west region month amount west jan 30 west feb 40 2 rows sales_all region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 west jan 30 west feb 40 4 rows note None entries in the list are skipped. A list that is None, empty, or empty once the None entries are dropped makes concat() return None, which leaves the output table on its current version instead of committing a new one. See concat for the full signature.
While TableFrames are typically received as input in publishers and transformers, you can also create them programmatically for testing or data generation purposes.

Use TableFrame.from_dict() to create a TableFrame from a Python dictionary: transform.py from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame data = { "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"], "age": [25, 30, 35], "city": ["New York", "London", "Paris"] } tf = TableFrame.from_dict(data)

Convert a Pandas DataFrame to a TableFrame: transform.py import pandas as pd from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame df = pd.DataFrame({ "product": ["Widget", "Gadget"], "price": [19.99, 29.99] }) tf = TableFrame.from_pandas(df)

Convert from Polars LazyFrame or DataFrame: transform.py import polars as pl from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame # From Polars LazyFrame lf = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(lf) # From Polars DataFrame pdf = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(pdf)

Export TableFrames to other formats: transform.py # To dictionary data_dict = tf.to_dict() # To Pandas DataFrame pandas_df = tf.to_pandas() # To Polars DataFrame polars_df = tf.to_polars_df() # To Polars LazyFrame polars_lf = tf.to_polars_lf() See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

A transformer reads one or more Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Joining two of them is the most common case: declare both under input_tables and the function takes a parameter for each. See Transformers for the anatomy of a transformer Function. Every block below joins the same two tables. orders has three rows and customers has three, overlapping on two customer_id values: o3 points at c9, which no customer has, and c3 has no order. What a join does with those two rows is the whole difference between the types.

Set the type with how. Every one of these joins on customer_id: innerleftrightfullsemianti Only the rows that match on both sides. The default. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "customers"], output_tables=["order_names"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(customers, on="customer_id") return result orders order_id customer_id amount o1 c1 10 o2 c2 20 o3 c9 5 3 rows customers customer_id name c1 Ada c2 Grace c3 Cy 3 rows order_names order_id customer_id amount name o1 c1 10 Ada o2 c2 20 Grace 2 rows

A key can span several columns, and the two sides can name them differently: on=[...]left_on / right_on One key spanning several columns. A row matches only when every column agrees. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["visits", "targets"], output_tables=["visits_vs_target"], ) def transform(visits: TableFrameSpec, targets: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = visits.join(targets, on=["customer_id", "date"]) return result visits customer_id date spend c1 mon 10 c2 mon 7 c1 tue 4 3 rows targets customer_id date target c1 mon 12 c2 mon 5 2 rows visits_vs_target customer_id date spend target c1 mon 10 12 c2 mon 7 5 2 rows

Before you begin Create a Project A CDC stream source reads a database's replication log and emits one Tabsdata table per tracked table. Every insert, update, and delete arrives, rather than whatever a SELECT happens to see when it runs. Three databases have a CDC source, each with its own connection type: Connection type Database Class mysql-cdc MySQL MySQLCdcStreamSrc postgres-cdc PostgreSQL PostgresCdcStreamSrc db2-cdc IBM Db2 Db2CdcStreamSrc What runs the publisher is a rollover rather than a clock or an upstream commit. The stream worker consumes the log continuously, and when a threshold trips it writes the buffer out and hands the batch to the publisher, which de-duplicates and offset-filters the rows before ingesting them. @stream_publisher takes no trigger_by. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-cdc.yaml Fill in the URI, the credentials, and the tables list, then create the collection: tdk collection create \ --name inventory \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-cdc.yaml All three CDC types register with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc @stream_publisher( source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=["shop.products", "shop.stock"], start_from="tail", ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["products", "stock"], ) def read_changes( products: TableFramesSpec, stock: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFramesSpec, TableFramesSpec]: return (products, stock) One output table per tracked table, in order, and one TableFramesSpec parameter per slot. The function must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll inventory \ --path read_changes.py::read_changes Registration starts the stream worker, which begins consuming the log.
documents.s: Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database

documents.t: start_from decides what the worker reads first. For PostgreSQL, "head" starts at the oldest retained WAL, "tail" starts at the current LSN, and an LsnPosition starts at a position you name. Starting at the tail skips the history and streams only what arrives from now on.

PostgreSQL logical replication is slot-based, so its connection carries fields the other two do not: Field Purpose replication_slot The slot name, required replication_slot_behavior "reuse" (default) or "create" publication_name Optional publication to read from columns_format "columns" (default), "struct", or "map" flatten_columns Defaults to True

flush_interval_mins is a fallback ceiling, minimum 1 whole minute. The connector's own thresholds in src_cfg cover buffer size and polling cadence, and whichever threshold trips first closes the batch, so the connector's window is usually the one that fires.

MySQL and PostgreSQL CDC both need a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Declare it during installation, as described in Installing Third-Party Database Drivers. Adding it later means re-running the installation.
Trigger off a Kafka Stream covers the fourth stream source, which follows the same rollover model against a topic. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run.

Before you begin Create a Project A CronTrigger runs a function at fixed times whether or not any upstream data changed. It is the right trigger for a publisher, which has nothing inside Tabsdata to signal that its external system has new rows. Tabsdata reads every crontab schedule in UTC. Step 1Add a CronTrigger to the function read_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import CronTrigger, TableFrameSpec, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders"], ), output_tables=["orders"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders "0 * * * *" fires at the top of every hour. The mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week, with minute precision. Extensions like @hourly and @daily are not supported. Mask When it runs 0,30 * * * * Every 30 minutes, on the hour and at minute 30 0 0 * * * Daily at 00:00 UTC 0 22 * * FRI Fridays at 22:00 UTC Step 2Register the function tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path read_orders.py::read_orders The schedule starts from the moment registration succeeds. Re-register with --update after any change to the mask. Step 3Confirm the schedule took tdk fn get --coll sales --name read_orders

start and end limit when the mask applies. Both take a timezone-aware Python datetime or an ISO 8601 string in UTC: trigger_by=CronTrigger( "0 * * * *", start="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", end="2026-04-01T00:00:00Z", ) Omit them and the mask applies indefinitely from registration.
documents.s: Bounding the schedule to a window

documents.t: A cron schedule only fires while its function is enabled, so pausing one is a matter of disabling the function rather than editing the mask: tdk fn disable --coll sales --name read_orders tdk fn enable --coll sales --name read_orders A disabled function keeps its registration and its mask, and Tabsdata ignores the mask until it is enabled again. Register a function --disabled to add it without starting its schedule.

A cron trigger fires on a clock regardless of upstream state. To run a function because data actually arrived, see Trigger a Function from a Table Commit. See Cron Triggers for how the trigger behaves.

Before you begin Create a Project A Kafka stream source consumes one topic continuously and emits a single Tabsdata table named after that topic. What runs the publisher is neither a clock nor an upstream commit but a rollover: the stream worker buffers messages, and when a rollover threshold trips it writes the buffer out as parquet and hands the batch to the publisher to ingest. @stream_publisher therefore takes no trigger_by at all. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type kafka-topic-in --file conn-kafka.yaml Fill in the bootstrap servers, then create the collection with it: tdk collection create \ --name events \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-kafka.yaml servers is the only required field. credentials is optional, so a broker that takes SASL gets a UserPassword block here and a broker without authentication gets none. The topic is not a connection field: it belongs to the source in the function, along with the message format and schema. A Kafka connection registers with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group like a plain source does. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_clicks.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc CLICK_SCHEMA = """ { "type": "record", "name": "Click", "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "url", "type": "string"}, {"name": "ts", "type": "long"} ] } """ @stream_publisher( source=KafkaStreamSrc( topic="clicks", data_format="json", schema=CLICK_SCHEMA, ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["clicks"], ) def read_clicks(clicks: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFramesSpec: return clicks The output table takes the topic's name, and there is always exactly one. schema is required, and in schema-registry mode it is cross-checked against the registry. The function takes one TableFramesSpec per source slot, always in array mode, and must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction, so no transaction context exists at the call boundary. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll events \ --path read_clicks.py::read_clicks Registration starts the stream worker. It consumes continuously from that point.

Rollover fires on whichever threshold trips first, the connector's own or the decorator's fallback. Kafka takes min(time_rollover_secs, flush_interval_mins * 60), so flush_interval_mins is a ceiling and the connector's window is usually the one that fires. Set the connector's thresholds in src_cfg: Key Closes the batch when kafka.time_rollover_seconds That many seconds have passed kafka.size_rollover_mb The buffer reaches that size kafka.messages_rollover That many messages have accumulated flush_interval_mins takes whole minutes, minimum 1.
Set dlq_topic on the source and Kafka messages that cannot be deserialized are routed there instead of failing the batch.

Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database covers the other three stream sources, which follow the same rollover model against a database log. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run, and Kafka for the full connector setup.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk fn trigger runs a registered function on demand. Any function can be triggered this way, including one that already carries a trigger_by schedule, so a manual trigger is how you test a function before trusting it to a cron mask. A publisher with no trigger_by runs only when triggered manually. That is the default for publishers, since nothing upstream inside Tabsdata can signal that an external system has new data. Step 1Trigger the function tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders The command waits for the plan to finish and reports each function as it completes. Pass --detach to return immediately instead. Step 2Check what the run produced tdk table list --coll sales tdk table data --coll sales --name orders

A trigger does not run one function in isolation. Tabsdata builds an execution plan covering every function downstream of the one you named, and runs them in dependency order: a transformer reading the publisher's output runs next, then a subscriber reading that transformer's output. Nothing commits unless every function in the plan succeeds. Name the plan to make it easier to find afterward: tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders \ --plan-name nightly-backfill
documents.s: Triggering runs more than one function

documents.t: tdk fnrun list --coll sales --fn read_orders The listing carries each run's id, which is what the log and recovery commands take: tdk fnrun logs --fnrun <run_id> tdk fnrun recover --fnrun <run_id> recover resumes the plan a failed run belongs to rather than starting a new one.

Automate it. Schedule a Cron Trigger runs the function on a clock, and Trigger a Function from a Table Commit runs it when an upstream table gets new data. See Manual Triggers for how the trigger behaves, and tdk fn trigger for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A table trigger runs a function whenever a table it watches receives a new commit. This is how a pipeline advances on its own: a publisher lands data, the transformer watching that table runs, and the subscriber watching the transformer's output runs after it. Transformers and subscribers already work this way without being told to. Omit trigger_by and a commit to any of the function's input tables triggers it. trigger_by is for the two cases the default does not cover: triggering off fewer tables than the function reads, and triggering off tables it does not read at all. Step 1Write the function against its input tables summarize.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["orders"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], ) def summarize(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders.group_by("region").agg(col("amount").sum()) With no trigger_by, a commit to orders runs this transformer. Step 2Register it tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path summarize.py::summarize Step 3Trigger the upstream function and watch the chain tdk fn trigger --coll sales --name read_orders The publisher commits orders, which triggers summarize in the same execution plan. Both appear in the run listing: tdk fnrun list --coll sales
documents.s: Trigger a Function from a Table Commit

documents.t: A commit to any input table triggers the function, and trigger_by narrows that set: @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "regions"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders"], ) regions is still read on every run and still supplies its current data. It no longer starts one, which suits a lookup table whose edits do not warrant recomputing the summary. This is not about avoiding duplicate runs. A plan that commits both orders and regions runs this transformer once either way, because the plan covers every downstream function and orders them by dependency rather than firing one run per committed table.

trigger_by accepts tables that are not inputs at all, which is how a function runs in response to something it does not consume: @transformer( input_tables=["orders"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders", "ops/refresh_signal"], ) A commit to ops/refresh_signal now runs the transformer, though it reads nothing from that table. A publisher uses the same mechanism: it has no input_tables at all, so a table reference in trigger_by is the only way a Tabsdata commit can start it. Reference a table outside the function's own collection as collection/table. Cross-collection references work within one project. A reference to a table in another project surfaces as Dependency table '<x>' does not exist, because row-level security hides it rather than reporting it as forbidden.
documents.s: Triggering off a table the function does not read

documents.t: An empty list disables it, leaving the function manual-only: trigger_by=[]

A publisher writing three tables commits all three on every run, whether or not the rows in a given table differ from last time, and every commit triggers whatever watches that table. A run that returns None for a table is the exception: that keeps the current version instead of committing a new one, so nothing downstream fires.
documents.s: A commit does not mean the data changed

documents.t: Schedule a Cron Trigger to run a function on a clock instead, which is what a publisher usually needs. See Table Commit Triggers for how the trigger behaves.
